problem: It says "ls is a utility, cd is a built-in, read is a system call". In bash, read is itself a built-in command (read name reads a line into a variable), so a student reading this trap concludes that typing read runs a system call. The trap then teaches the opposite of what it intends.
fix: Use a name that is unambiguously a system call, e.g. "ls is a utility, cd is a built-in, and getpid or write(2) is a system call; bash also has a built-in called read, which is not the read(2) system call." When the kernel entry point is meant, write read(2) with the section number.

where: Section 2, "A command can be one of four things"
problem: The list has built-ins, external commands, aliases and functions, but omits shell reserved words and keywords (if, for, while, {, [[). These are also commands as far as the shell's parser is concerned, and bash resolves a command line in five kinds, not four.
fix: Say "the shell looks at a command line in this order: alias, reserved word or keyword such as if and while, function, built-in, then an external file found in PATH" and keep the four explanations as the common cases.

problem: argv is called "the argument list" without saying that by convention argv[0] is the program name, so the traced call execve('/bin/ls', argv, envp) looks like it passes only the word ls. A student may think argv holds just the typed words.
fix: Add: argv[0] is the command name "ls", the remaining entries are the arguments, and envp holds the environment strings NAME=value.
